title: Common Types of Synthetic Rubber

body_markdown:
Synthetic rubber is a polymer-based elastomer produced through the chemical polymerization of petroleum-derived monomers. Synthetic rubber functions as a group of engineered elastomers formulated to meet specific mechanical, thermal, and chemical performance demands across industrial sectors. The formulations range from general-purpose compounds to specialized grades engineered for extreme temperature, fuel resistance, and weathering conditions. Industries (automotive, aerospace, construction, and medical manufacturing) rely on distinct synthetic rubber types, depending on application load and environmental exposure.


The common types of synthetic rubber are listed below.


- **Styrene Butadiene Rubber (SBR)** : A copolymer of styrene (23% to 25%) and butadiene, delivering abrasion resistance and tensile strength ranging from 15 to 20 MPa in reinforced form. SBR acts as the standard material in passenger tire treads, conveyor belts, and shoe soles.
- **Nitrile Rubber (NBR)** : An acrylonitrile-butadiene copolymer with acrylonitrile content ranging from 18% to 50%, maintaining a service temperature from -40°C to 120°C. NBR acts as the primary elastomer in fuel hoses, O-rings, and oil-resistant gaskets.
- **Neoprene (Polychloroprene)** : A polychloroprene-based elastomer offering balanced resistance to weathering, ozone, and moderate chemical exposure. Neoprene retains flexibility across a service temperature range from -40°C to 120°C, finding application in wetsuits, cable jacketing, and industrial hose covers.
- **Ethylene Propylene Diene Monomer (EPDM)** : A terpolymer of ethylene, propylene, and a diene monomer, operating reliably from -50°C to 150°C. EPDM acts as the dominant elastomer in roofing membranes, automotive door seals, and outdoor weatherstripping.
- **Butyl Rubber (IIR)** : An isobutylene-isoprene copolymer with exceptionally low gas permeability, operating from -50°C to 120°C. IIR serves in tubeless tire inner liners, pharmaceutical stoppers, and steam hose applications.
- **Silicone Rubber (VMQ)** : A polysiloxane-based elastomer maintaining flexibility across a temperature range from -60°C to 230°C. VMQ serves in medical-grade tubing, aerospace seals, and electronic encapsulation components.
- **Polybutadiene Rubber (BR)** : A homopolymer of butadiene with the highest resilience and lowest heat buildup of all synthetic rubber grades, operating from -100°C to 100°C. BR functions as a primary blending component in tire sidewalls and high-impact-resistant polymer systems.


## 1. Styrene Butadiene Rubber (SBR)


Styrene Butadiene Rubber (SBR) is a synthetic rubber copolymer derived from styrene and butadiene monomers, carrying a monomer composition of 23% to 25% styrene and 75% to 77% butadiene. First developed in Germany in 1929 as a substitute for natural rubber, SBR ranks as the most consumed synthetic rubber in global industrial production. The rubber delivers a service temperature range from -40°C to 82°C, with tensile strength reaching 15 to 20 MPa in carbon black-reinforced form. A higher styrene content increases hardness and wear resistance, while a higher butadiene content improves flexibility and low-temperature performance. Primary applications cover passenger tire treads, conveyor belts, shoe soles, flooring, and industrial gaskets, establishing Styrene Butadiene Rubber as a foundational material across automotive and manufacturing sectors.


## 2. Nitrile Rubber (NBR)


Nitrile Rubber (NBR) is a synthetic elastomer produced through the copolymerization of acrylonitrile (ACN) and butadiene, with acrylonitrile content ranging from 15% to 50% depending on the target application. First patented in 1934 by German chemists Erich Konrad and Eduard Tschunkur under the trade name Buna-N, NBR gained widespread industrial adoption due to its resistance to petroleum-based oils, fuels, and chemicals. The acrylonitrile content directly determines oil resistance and gas permeability, where higher ACN concentrations improve chemical resistance but reduce low-temperature flexibility. NBR maintains a service temperature range from -40°C to 120°C, with tensile strength and abrasion resistance suited for high-wear sealing environments. Primary applications cover fuel hoses, O-rings, oil seals, hydraulic gaskets, drilling equipment, and disposable gloves across automotive, oil and gas, aerospace, and medical manufacturing sectors, establishing Nitrile Rubber (NBR) as the dominant oil-resistant elastomer in global industrial production.


## 3. Neoprene (Polychloroprene)


Neoprene is a synthetic elastomer produced through the polymerization of chloroprene (2-chloro-1,3-butadiene), resulting in a polychloroprene polymer with balanced mechanical and chemical performance. First developed in 1930 by American chemist Arnold Collins at DuPont and commercially marketed as Neoprene, the material reached an annual global production of 300,000 tons. The chlorine content in its molecular structure provides inherent flame resistance, moderate oil resistance, and strong ozone and UV stability. Neoprene maintains a service temperature range from -40°C to 121°C, retaining flexibility and structural integrity across outdoor and industrial environments. Primary applications cover wetsuits, cable jacketing, automotive gaskets, industrial conveyor belts, adhesives, and nuclear plant membrane valves, establishing Neoprene as a reliable general-purpose elastomer across marine, construction, and automotive sectors.


## 4. Ethylene Propylene Diene Monomer (EPDM)


Ethylene Propylene Diene Monomer (EPDM) is a synthetic thermoset rubber composed of ethylene (45% to 85%), propylene, and a non-conjugated diene monomer at 3% to 9%, produced through solution or emulsion polymerization. The saturated hydrocarbon backbone of EPDM delivers outstanding resistance to UV radiation, ozone, weathering, water, and steam, outperforming general-purpose elastomers in outdoor environments. EPDM operates reliably from -50°C to 150°C, maintaining flexibility and sealing integrity across extreme thermal cycles. The diene component provides crosslinking sites for sulfur vulcanization, improving mechanical strength and compression set resistance. Primary applications cover roofing membranes, automotive door and window seals, wire and cable insulation, and industrial hose systems, positioning Ethylene Propylene Diene Monomer (EPDM) as the dominant elastomer in weathering-critical engineering applications.


## 5. Butyl Rubber (IIR)


Butyl Rubber (IIR) is a synthetic elastomer produced through low-temperature cationic copolymerization of isobutylene ( 98%) with a small amount of isoprene ( 2%), forming an isobutylene-isoprene rubber with a predominantly saturated backbone. IIR holds the distinction of being the known elastomer that does not transmit gases, delivering exceptionally low gas and moisture permeability across industrial sealing applications developed in 1937. The saturated backbone structure provides outstanding resistance to ozone, UV radiation, heat aging, and dilute acids and alkalis, with a service temperature range from -50°C to 120°C. Halogenated grades (CIIR and BIIR) developed in the 1960s further improved curing rates and adhesion properties. Primary applications cover tubeless tire inner liners, pharmaceutical vial stoppers, steam hoses, gas-tight membranes, and construction sealants, establishing Butyl Rubber (IIR) as the standard elastomer in airtight and moisture-barrier engineering systems.


## 6. Silicone Rubber (VMQ)


Silicone Rubber (VMQ), formally designated as Vinyl Methyl Silicone, is a polysiloxane-based elastomer composed of silicon, oxygen, carbon, and hydrogen, forming a high molecular weight polymer backbone with vinyl groups added to improve crosslinking and mechanical performance. VMQ carries an inorganic siloxane backbone that delivers thermal stability across a service temperature range from -60°C to 230°C, with specialty grades extending performance beyond 300°C, unlike carbon-based elastomers. VMQ maintains flexibility, electrical insulation, and chemical resistance across cryogenic and high-temperature environments where organic rubbers fail. Its biocompatibility, odorless nature, and non-toxicity qualify it for food-grade, pharmaceutical, and medical-grade applications. Primary applications cover aerospace seals, medical tubing, electronic encapsulation, automotive engine gaskets, and food processing components, establishing Silicone Rubber (VMQ) as the preferred high-performance elastomer in temperature-critical and biocompatible engineering systems.


## 7. Polybutadiene Rubber (BR)


Polybutadiene Rubber (BR) is a synthetic elastomer produced through solution polymerization of 1,3-butadiene, yielding a high cis-1,4-microstructure content of 90% to 98% that governs its elastic and mechanical performance. BR ranks as the second most consumed synthetic rubber globally, with annual demand exceeding 2.8 million metric tons, driven by the tire industry, which accounts for over 70% of total BR consumption. The glass transition temperature ranges from -95°C to -110°C, giving BR the highest low-temperature flexibility among commercial synthetic rubbers. Its low heat buildup, superior resilience, and crack growth resistance make it the dominant blending component in tire tread and sidewall compounds. Primary applications cover passenger tire compounds, golf ball cores, conveyor belts, shoe soles, and high-impact ABS plastic modification, establishing Polybutadiene Rubber (BR) as a foundational elastomer in high-resilience and wear-critical industrial systems.


### How Do the Different Types of Synthetic Rubber Compare in Performance?


The performance of synthetic rubber types varies significantly across temperature tolerance, chemical resistance, weathering durability, and cost. Each elastomer grade carries a distinct property profile that determines its suitability across automotive, industrial, medical, and construction applications. Selecting the correct synthetic rubber grade depends on the operating environment, chemical exposure, and mechanical load requirements. Silicone (VMQ) leads the widest temperature range from -60°C to 230°C, while Nitrile Butadiene Rubber (NBR) holds the strongest oil resistance rating among all grades. Ethylene Propylene Diene Monomer (EPDM) and Butyl (IIR) deliver the highest weathering resistance, favoring outdoor and airtight sealing applications. SBR and BR carry the lowest cost index, dominating high-volume tire and footwear manufacturing sectors.


The different types of synthetic rubber compared in performance are shown in the table below.


### Which Type of Synthetic Rubber Has the Best Heat Resistance?


The types of synthetic rubber that have the best heat resistance are listed below.


- **Silicone Rubber (VMQ)** : The highest heat-resistant synthetic rubber grade, maintaining flexibility from -60°C to 230°C, with specialty formulations exceeding 300°C in aerospace and medical sealing applications.
- **Ethylene Propylene Diene Monomer (EPDM)** : Operates from -50°C to 150°C, retaining ozone and weathering resistance at elevated temperatures across outdoor and automotive sealing systems.
- **Neoprene (Polychloroprene)** : Sustains a service temperature from -40°C to 121°C with retained flame and ozone resistance, suiting cable jacketing and industrial belting applications.
- **Nitrile Butadiene Rubber (NBR)** : Operates from -40°C to 120°C, combining oil resistance with adequate thermal stability in fuel and hydraulic sealing environments.
- **Butyl Rubber (IIR)** : Maintains performance from -50°C to 120°C with strong resistance to thermal oxidation in steam hose and pharmaceutical closure applications.
- **Styrene Butadiene Rubber (SBR)** : Operates from -40°C to 82°C, limited in high-temperature applications but dominant in tire treads and conveyor belt systems.
- **Polybutadiene Rubber (BR)** : The lowest upper heat threshold at 100°C, compensating with the highest low-temperature flexibility at -95°C in tire sidewall and polymer blending applications.


### Which Synthetic Rubber is Most Resistant to Chemicals?


The most resistant synthetic rubbers to chemicals are listed below.


- **Nitrile Butadiene Rubber (NBR)** : The strongest oil and fuel-resistant grade, withstanding petroleum-based oils, gasoline, diesel, and hydraulic fluids across acrylonitrile content ranging from 18% to 50%.
- **Neoprene (Polychloroprene)** : Delivers moderate resistance to oils, greases, acids, and refrigerants, with chlorine content providing inherent chemical stability across a broad exposure range.
- **Butyl Rubber (IIR)** : Resistant to acids, alkalis, polar solvents, and ketone-based hydraulic fluids, performing poorly against petroleum-based oils and hydrocarbon solvents.
- **Ethylene Propylene Diene Monomer (EPDM)** : Resistant to water, steam, polar solvents, and dilute acids, performing poorly against petroleum-based oils and hydrocarbon fuels.
- **Silicone Rubber (VMQ)** : Resistant to dilute acids, alkalis, ozone, and UV exposure, with limited resistance to concentrated acids, fuels, and hydrocarbon solvents.
- **Styrene Butadiene Rubber (SBR)** : Resistant to water, dilute acids, and alcohols, showing poor resistance to oils, fuels, and concentrated chemical agents.
- **Polybutadiene Rubber (BR)** : The lowest chemical resistance among major grades, offering adequate performance against water and dilute inorganic acids.


## What Are the Main Uses of Synthetic Rubber Across Industries?


The main uses of synthetic rubber across industries are listed below.


- **Automotive Industry** : Synthetic rubber serves in fuel hoses, oil seals, door seals, timing belts, and tire compounds across passenger and commercial vehicle production. Nitrile Butadiene Rubber dominates oil-contact components, while Ethylene Propylene Diene Monomer covers weatherstripping and door seals.
- **Tire Manufacturing** : Styrene Butadiene Rubber and Polybutadiene Rubber function as the primary compounds in tire treads and sidewalls, accounting for over 70% of global Polybutadiene Rubber consumption. Butyl Rubber (IIR) serves exclusively in tubeless tire inner liners due to its unmatched gas impermeability.
- **Aerospace and Defense** : Silicone Rubber (VMQ) and specialty fluorosilicone grades seal fuel tanks, hydraulic systems, and structural joints operating across extreme temperature ranges. Neoprene serves in self-sealing fuel tank liners and cable jacketing across military and aviation platforms.
- **Construction and Infrastructure** : Ethylene Propylene Diene Monomer dominates roofing membrane systems, expansion joint seals, and waterproofing layers in commercial building structures. Butyl Rubber serves in construction sealants, flashing tapes, and gas-tight membrane systems requiring long-term weather resistance.
- **Medical and Pharmaceutical** : Silicone Rubber (VMQ) provides biocompatible tubing, seals, and encapsulation components across medical device and surgical equipment production. Butyl Rubber (IIR) functions as the standard pharmaceutical vial stopper material due to its chemical inertness and gas impermeability.
- **Oil and Gas Industry** : Nitrile Butadiene Rubber serves in blowout preventers, packers, drilling equipment seals, and pipeline gaskets exposed to hydrocarbons and elevated pressure. Ethylene Propylene Diene Monomer covers above-ground sealing systems exposed to weathering and steam in refinery environments.
- **Electronics and Electrical Systems** : Silicone Rubber (VMQ) provides wire and cable insulation, connector seals, and electromagnetic interference shielding across industrial and consumer electronics manufacturing. Styrene Butadiene Rubber serves in cable insulation and electrical gasket applications requiring moderate chemical resistance at a lower cost.


### How Is Synthetic Rubber Used in the Automotive Industry?


Synthetic rubber serves in the automotive industry as a primary material for sealing, vibration damping, fuel management, and structural bonding components. Nitrile Butadiene Rubber covers fuel hoses, oil seals, and O-rings due to its resistance to petroleum-based fluids, while Ethylene Propylene Diene Monomer covers door seals, window weatherstripping, and radiator hoses from -50°C to 150°C. Neoprene provides transmission belts, engine mounts, and vibration isolators where moderate oil and heat resistance are required simultaneously.


Styrene Butadiene Rubber and Polybutadiene Rubber form the primary tire tread and sidewall compounds, with Polybutadiene Rubber accounting for over 70% of tire sidewall elastomer consumption globally. Butyl Rubber (IIR) serves in tubeless tire inner liners, retaining air pressure and minimizing steel belt corrosion due to its gas impermeability. Silicone Rubber (VMQ) covers high-temperature engine gaskets, ignition cable insulation, and sensor seals operating continuously above 150°C in modern internal combustion and electric vehicle systems.


### How Is Synthetic Rubber Used in Medical and Healthcare Applications?


Synthetic rubber is used in medical and healthcare applications as a primary material for biocompatible sealing, fluid management, protective equipment, and implantable device components. Silicone Rubber (VMQ) dominates medical-grade applications due to its biocompatibility, non-toxicity, and thermal stability from -60°C to 230°C, meeting FDA, USP Class VI, and ISO 10993 certification standards. Nitrile Butadiene Rubber serves in disposable examination gloves, surgical gloves, and laboratory protective gear, replacing natural latex due to its lower allergenic risk and puncture resistance across acrylonitrile content ranging from 18% to 50%.


Silicone Rubber (VMQ) provides medical-grade tubing, catheters, implant-grade sheeting, and drainage systems where long-term biological compatibility and sterilization resistance are required. Butyl Rubber (IIR) functions as the standard pharmaceutical vial and injection stopper material, maintaining gas impermeability and chemical inertness across repeated needle penetration cycles. Silicone-based implants cover reconstructive and corrective medical procedures requiring durable, flexible, and non-reactive materials in direct tissue contact environments. Nitrile Butadiene Rubber further extends into laboratory tubing, fluid transfer lines, and diagnostic equipment seals across clinical and research healthcare facilities.


#### Is Synthetic Rubber Safe for Food Contact Applications?


Yes, synthetic rubber is safe for food contact applications. The safety rating depends on the grade, formulation, and regulatory certification of the elastomer. Silicone Rubber (VMQ) functions as the primary food-contact elastomer, meeting FDA 21 CFR, EU 10/2011, and NSF 51 certification standards across baking mats, food processing seals, and beverage tubing. Butyl Rubber (IIR) qualifies for food-contact closures in pharmaceutical and food-grade bottle stopper applications due to its chemical inertness and odorless composition. Nitrile Butadiene Rubber requires specific food-grade compounding certification before qualifying for direct food contact, as residual acrylonitrile content above permissible limits disqualifies standard industrial grades. Styrene Butadiene Rubber, Neoprene, and Polybutadiene Rubber carry limited food-contact suitability, requiring independent formulation testing and regulatory approval, depending on additive composition and intended application.


## How to Choose the Right Type of Synthetic Rubber for a Specific Application?


To choose the right type of synthetic rubber for a specific application, follow the seven steps listed below.


1. **Identify the Operating Temperature Range** . Determine the minimum and maximum service temperatures the elastomer encounters. Silicone Rubber (VMQ) suits extreme ranges from -60°C to 230°C, while Styrene Butadiene Rubber covers moderate ranges from -40°C to 82°C.
2. **Evaluate Chemical Exposure Requirements** . Identify the specific chemicals, fluids, and solvents the elastomer contacts during service. Nitrile Butadiene Rubber suits petroleum-based oil and fuel exposure, while Ethylene Propylene Diene Monomer suits water, steam, and polar solvent environments.
3. **Assess Mechanical Load and Wear Conditions** . Determine the pressure, friction, and dynamic stress levels the elastomer must withstand continuously. Polybutadiene Rubber suits high-resilience applications, while Butyl Rubber (IIR) suits low-dynamic, high-damping sealing systems.
4. **Determine Weathering and UV Exposure Levels** . Evaluate whether the elastomer faces prolonged outdoor exposure to ozone, UV radiation, and moisture. Ethylene Propylene Diene Monomer and Butyl Rubber (IIR) deliver the highest weathering resistance among major synthetic rubber grades.
5. **Check Regulatory and Safety Certification Requirements** . Confirm whether the application requires food-grade, medical-grade, or industry-specific compliance certifications. Silicone Rubber (VMQ) meets FDA 21 CFR, USP Class VI, and NSF 51 standards for food contact and medical device applications.
6. **Compare Cost Index Against Performance Requirements** . Balance material cost against the mechanical and chemical performance demands of the application. Styrene Butadiene Rubber and Polybutadiene Rubber carry the lowest cost index, while Silicone Rubber (VMQ) carries the highest.
7. **Validate Through Application-Specific Testing** . Conduct compression set, tensile strength, chemical swell, and aging resistance testing before full-scale deployment. Validation testing confirms elastomer suitability across the actual service conditions of the application.


### What Factors Affect the Performance of Synthetic Rubber in Extreme Conditions?


The factors that affect the performance of synthetic rubber in extreme conditions are temperature extremes, chemical concentration, UV exposure duration, and mechanical compression. Silicone Rubber (VMQ) retains flexibility from -60°C to 230°C, while Styrene Butadiene Rubber loses mechanical integrity above 82°C under continuous thermal load. Styrene Butadiene Rubber and Nitrile Butadiene Rubber show measurable surface cracking after 500 to 1,000 hours of outdoor UV exposure without protective additives.


Nitrile Butadiene Rubber at 50% acrylonitrile content retains dimensional stability in full-concentration petroleum fluid immersion, while lower acrylonitrile grades swell beyond acceptable limits above 40% fluid concentration. Compression set accumulation reduces sealing force over time, with Nitrile Butadiene Rubber showing values ranging from 20% to 40% after 70 hours at 100°C, depending on compound formulation. Silicone Rubber (VMQ) maintains the lowest long-term compression set among major synthetic rubber grades, retaining sealing integrity across repeated thermal cycling in aerospace and medical device applications.


### What Is the Cost Range for Different Types of Synthetic Rubber?


The cost range for different types of synthetic rubber spans from \[$ 1.50 to $ 45.00\] per kilogram, varying from commodity-grade elastomers to specialty high-performance compounds. Styrene Butadiene Rubber and Polybutadiene Rubber carry the lowest market price, ranging from \[$ 1.50 to $ 2.50\] per kilogram, reflecting their petroleum-derived monomer availability and high-volume production scale. Nitrile Butadiene Rubber prices range from \[$ 2.50 to $ 5.00\] per kilogram, depending on acrylonitrile content, with higher acrylonitrile grades commanding premium pricing due to improved oil resistance performance.


Neoprene (Polychloroprene) and Ethylene Propylene Diene Monomer fall in the mid-range from \[$ 3.00 to $ 6.00\] per kilogram, depending on grade, formulation additives, and vulcanization requirements. Butyl Rubber (IIR) ranges from \[$ 2.80 to $ 5.50\] per kilogram, with halogenated grades (CIIR and BIIR) carrying a price premium of 15% to 25% above standard IIR grades. Silicone Rubber (VMQ) carries the highest cost index among major synthetic rubber grades, ranging from \[$ 8.00 to $ 45.00\] per kilogram, depending on purity level, medical-grade certification, and specialty formulation requirements.


#### Can Synthetic Rubber Be Recycled or Is It Environmentally Harmful?


Yes, synthetic rubber is recyclable, but the cross-linked molecular structure of vulcanized elastomers makes conventional recycling processes difficult to apply on an industrial scale. Mechanical recycling through cryogenic grinding produces crumb rubber at particle sizes ranging from 0.5 mm to 4 mm, repurposed in playground surfaces, athletic tracks, and asphalt modification systems. Pyrolysis processing at temperatures ranging from 300°C to 700°C breaks down vulcanized rubber into recovered carbon black, pyrolysis oil, and combustible gas, recovering 40% to 60% of the original material energy content. Devulcanization techniques targeting sulfur crosslink bonds restore partial elastomeric properties, allowing recycled rubber to re-enter compounding processes at substitution rates of 10% to 30%, depending on grade and application requirements. Unrecycled synthetic rubber in landfills presents long-term environmental concerns, as vulcanized elastomers resist biodegradation for periods exceeding 50 to 80 years under standard soil conditions.
